theme: 3 terms on collections that hold many values

terms.definition: An ordered collection of values of the same type that you read by their position, starting at zero.
terms.example: I stored the photo names in an array so the gallery shows them in the same order every time.
terms.code:
let names = ["a.png", "b.png", "c.png"]
print(names[0])   // starts at zero
print(names.count)

terms.definition: A collection that stores values under unique keys, so you look up a value by its key instead of its position.
terms.example: We keep the user settings in a dictionary, so I can read the theme by its key.
terms.code:
var ui = ["theme": "dark", "font": "big"]
ui["theme"] = "light"  // by key
print(ui["theme"] ?? "none")

terms.definition: An unordered collection of unique values, where each value can appear only once.
terms.example: I switched the selected tags to a set so the same tag can never be added twice.
terms.code:
var tags: Set = ["swift", "ios"]
tags.insert("swift")  // no change
print(tags.count)

Hi everyone, welcome to Day 5 of iOS Daily English!

Today we look at 3 Swift collections:

Array - an ordered list of values you read by position, starting at zero.
Dictionary - values stored under unique keys, so you look them up by key.
Set - unique values only, with no guaranteed order.

Every example sentence is read twice, once at normal speed and once slowly, so you can say it out loud with me.

dialogue.title: Sprint planning: data for the photo gallery

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Okay, sprint planning. Our topic is the photo gallery. How do we store the photos?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I suggest an array of file names. The gallery shows them in the same order every time.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Good. An array is ordered, and we read an item by its position.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: The first photo is at position one, right?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Not quite. An array starts at zero. So the first photo is names[0].

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Oh, right. I always make that mistake. An array with nine photos crashes if I read position ten.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. Next, the user settings, like the theme and the font size.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: That is a dictionary. We store each value under a key, like theme.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: So we do not need a position. We ask the dictionary for the theme.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the result is an optional, because the dictionary may not have that key.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Correct. Now the tags. Users can pick tags like travel and food.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: I think an array is fine for tags, too.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: I disagree. With an array the same tag can be added twice. A set keeps every value unique.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Good point. And I do not need the order of tags anyway.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. A set has no order, so it is a good fit.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Okay. I will use a set for the selected tags.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Last check. Does the gallery look the same after a restart?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Yes. The array keeps the photo order, so nothing moves.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Great. An array for photos, a dictionary for settings, a set for tags.
I stored the photo names in an array, so the order stays.
